name: Ekteswar Temple
significance: A laterite Shiva temple about 45 feet high on the bank of the Dwarakeswar river some 10 km from Bankura town, raised by the Malla king Raghunath Singha Dev in the 17th century. It is said to have been built as a token of unity after a boundary dispute between the kingdoms of Mallabhum and Samantabhum.
story: Local tradition holds that Shiva himself meditated at the spot to settle the boundary quarrel between the two kingdoms.

name: Kalugasalamoorthy Temple
builtDisplay: 18th c. halls on an early Pandya rock-cut core
significance: A hill temple at Kalugumalai whose core is early Pandya rock-cut work, with its images installed and pillared halls added in the 18th century. It was long controlled by the Ettaiyapuram zamindar and is now run by the Tamil Nadu HR&CE board; its 1895 Panguni Uthiram procession was the flashpoint of a deadly caste riot.
story: The sage Kalugumahamunivar, identified with Sampati the brother of Jatayu, is said to have helped Murugan against the demons Surapadman and Tarukasuran and to have won liberation here, giving the hill its name.

name: Thirupparankundram Rock-cut Cave Temple
significance: A rock-cut Shaiva shrine on the south face of Skandamalai near Madurai, its earliest excavation dated to the 8th-century early Pandya period and enlarged under Maravarman Sundara Pandya in the 13th century. An inscription there records tax-free land granted for its upkeep, and the cave is a protected national monument carrying reliefs of the Shaiva saints Appar, Sambandar and Siruthondar.

name: Billeswar Devalaya
significance: A Shiva temple at Belsor in Assam's Nalbari district, held to be about five centuries old. Maha Shivaratri and Durga Puja are its principal festivals, the latter still marked by the temple's long-standing buffalo sacrifice.

name: Varadharaja Perumal Temple, Puducherry
significance: A Vishnu temple in Puducherry town believed to have been founded by the Cholas in the 11th century and enlarged by the Pandyas in the 12th, later rebuilt in the colonial period. It sheltered the images of the Vedapurishvarar temple when that shrine was destroyed in 1748, and its Vasantha mandapa was funded jointly by the town's Hindu, Muslim and Christian residents.

name: Alamchandi Temple
significance: A Shakta shrine near the Atharanala bridge in Puri, dated on structural grounds to the later 16th century, with a natamandapa added in the 20th. It is counted among the Ashtashaktis that guard the sacred precinct of Srikshetra, and the logs cut for the Nabakalebara rite are first set down before it.

name: Bathu Temples
significance: A group of stone temples near Dhameta in Kangra district, dated by historical accounts to the 8th century, of which nine of the original eleven survive. They were submerged by the Maharana Pratap Sagar reservoir when the Pong dam filled in the early 1970s and emerge only between March and June as the water drops.
story: Local folklore credits the Pandavas with building them during their exile, and with abandoning a staircase meant to link the site to the Masrur rock temples in a single night — forty steps of it are still there.

name: Jagannath Temple, Rayagada
significance: A Jagannath temple on the southern edge of Rayagada town, known locally as Sradhha Shrikhetra. The older shrine was replaced by the present Kalinga-style structure, inaugurated on 20 June 2007 in the presence of the Gajapati Raja of Puri.

name: Bhimeshvara Temple, Nilagunda
significance: A soapstone Shiva temple at Nilagunda with four sanctums, dated by the Archaeological Survey of India to the last quarter of the 11th century, though the historian Adam Hardy places it in the 12th. Its non-mainstream Later Chalukya idiom carries Hoysala touches, and it is protected as a monument of national importance.

name: Malleswar Temple
significance: A square deul-form Shiva temple at Bishnupur, 6.9 metres to a side and 10.7 metres tall, founded in 1622 by the Mallabhum king Bir Singha. Its original curved rekha tower was later replaced by an octagonal one, and the temple is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

name: Jagatnagar Kalibari
significance: A Kali temple at Jagatnagar near Singur in Hooghly district, about 34 km from Kolkata, where the goddess is worshipped as Anandamayi Kali Ma.

name: Parshvanath Jain Temples, Varanasi
significance: A cluster of three Jain shrines at Bhelupur in Varanasi — a Digambara temple, a Shvetambara temple and the Parshvanatha–Padmavati temple. The Digambara shrine's worshipped black stone image of Parshvanatha, about 75 cm high, belongs to a group of sculptures found here dating from the 9th to 11th centuries CE.
story: Jains identify Bhelupur as the place of three of Parshvanatha's kalyanakas — his conception, birth and renunciation — in the city his father King Ashvasena is said to have ruled.

name: Vandevi Temple
significance: A temple to the forest goddess Vandevi about 6 km from Renukoot in Sonbhadra district, completed in 1953 around an image unearthed during the building of the Rihand dam. Navaratri and the month of Sawan draw its largest gatherings.

name: Buddhanath Temple
significance: A 12th-century Shiva temple at Garedi Panchana in Balipatna block, some 22 km from Bhubaneswar, attributed to king Chodaganga Dev and laid out on Tantric principles. It was renovated recently with 14th Finance Commission funds.
story: It is believed locally that a snakebite victim brought into the temple precinct will not die.

name: Jain Temple, Alappuzha
style: Jain, in Rajasthan stone and white marble
significance: The Jain temple on Gujarati Street in Alappuzha serves the community descended from forty-two Jain families brought from Kutch to help build up the port town under Dewan Raja Kesavadas. Its two shrines were restored in February 1994, and it holds an image of the 23rd Tirthankara unearthed in Kuttanad, evidence of Jainism's older presence in Kerala.

name: Dimapur Jain Temple
significance: A Digambara Jain temple on Jain Temple Road in Dimapur, built in 1947 by four members of the Sethi and Chabra families who had moved down from Kohima in 1944 to escape the Japanese advance. A rear section was added in 1989 and consecrated with a Panch Kalyanak ceremony.

name: Narasimha Jharni
significance: A cave temple at Bidar reached by wading some 300 metres along a water-filled tunnel cut under the Manichoola hills, where Narasimha is worshipped alongside a Shiva linga. It is counted among the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams of the Vaishnava tradition.
story: The demon Jharasura, slain by Narasimha, is said to have turned into water that has flowed from the god's feet through the tunnel ever since.

name: Jagannatha Perumal Temple, Tirumazhisai
significance: A Vishnu temple at Tirumazhisai near Chennai, one of the 108 Abhimana Kshetrams and revered as the birthplace of the Alvar Thirumalisai. Its oldest inscription dates from the reign of Kulothunga Chola III, and later grants record patronage by Kopperunjinga and by the Vijayanagara rulers Harihara Raya II and Virupaksha Raya II.
story: The Saptarishis are said to have asked to see the middle Jagannatha, and Vishnu appeared here between Vada Jagannatha at Puri and Keezha Jagannatha at Thirupullani.

name: Chaturmukha Basadi, Karkala
deity: The Tirthankaras Aranatha, Mallinatha and Munisuvrata
significance: A four-sided Jain basadi built in 1586 by Immadi Bhairarasa Vodeya on Chikkabetta hill at Karkala, near the Gommateshwara monolith. Its square granite hall opens through pillared porticoes on all four sides under a roof of massive slabs, and a contemporary inscription describes the building by its four symmetrical faces and records the village grants endowed for its worship.

name: Yoga Madhava Temple, Settikere
significance: A soapstone Vishnu temple at Settikere in Tumkur district, built in 1261 CE by an officer of the Hoysala empire under king Narasimha III. It follows a three-shrine plan on a raised jagati platform, with the central vimana laid out on a semi-stellate ground.
